content.text: When your server fetches a URL a user chose, the request leaves from inside your network, with your server's access. That's the whole attack: the user borrows that position to reach internal services and cloud metadata. Checking the URL text doesn't help, because many spellings, DNS records and redirects lead to the same internal address. Allow-list destinations when you can; otherwise check the resolved IP at connect time, turn off redirects and restrict egress.

A marketplace lets sellers import a product photo by pasting its URL. The server downloads the file, stores it and shows a preview. A security researcher pastes an internal address instead of a photo, and the "preview" comes back as JSON from an internal admin service, configuration included. The team had blocked
localhost
and
weeks earlier. Her URL used neither.
The common misconception
The belief: fetching a user-supplied URL from the server is harmless, because the request comes from inside our own network.

It sounds like the safe side of the firewall. The code is yours, it runs on your server, and the request is a plain GET for an image. Users can't reach your internal services, so the reasoning goes that nothing they type can either. Many teams add a quick check on the URL, block the obvious internal names and move on.
The flaw is in which side of the firewall matters. "Inside our own network" isn't the reassurance; it's the problem.
What actually happens
Your server becomes the attacker's proxy
OWASP's SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet describes
SSRF

as "an attack vector that abuses an application to interact with the internal/external network or the machine itself", and names the usual features: avatar images from a URL, webhooks and internal calls built from user data. Its HR example puts it plainly: "The user leverages the web application as a proxy to the HR system." OWASP's community page lists what's typically reachable: "AWS metadata", "internal services like http enabled databases", and internal endpoints "which are not intended to be exposed". Internal services often trust the network: if a database is "expected to only be available to internally, authentication may be disabled".
It's an access control failure

In the OWASP Top 10:2025, SSRF has no category of its own. A01:2025 Broken Access Control lists "CWE-918 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)" among its notable weaknesses. The framing fits: your server's network position is a privilege, and SSRF lets any user borrow it, much like the IDOR article earlier in this path described a user borrowing another user's data.
The URL text isn't the destination
A string check sees what the user typed. The connection goes wherever DNS and the network send it.
System.Uri
does normalize some spellings: in our test,
became
and the string check caught it. But
, the same
loopback

address written as IPv6, passed straight through, and so would any hostname whose DNS record points inside. Redirects are another way around: OWASP says to "Disable the support for the following of the redirection in your web client". And
DNS rebinding

defeats checks that resolve the name once and connect later: "Validate the resolved destination IP addresses against the application's permitted networks, then ensure the HTTP client connects only to validated addresses."
Cloud metadata is the classic target
OWASP notes that "In cloud environments SSRF is often used to access and steal credentials and access tokens from metadata services". On AWS, the
instance metadata service

has two versions, and "By default, you can use either IMDSv1 or IMDSv2, or both." IMDSv2 is session-oriented: a token must first be requested with a PUT, and "PUT requests are rejected if they contain an X-Forwarded-For header." AWS lets you configure instances to "only accept IMDSv2 calls, which will cause IMDSv1 calls to fail."
From a string check to a connection check

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: ConnectCallback

is, in Microsoft's words, "a custom callback used to open new connections", so the check runs on the exact addresses the socket uses, every time a connection opens. We ran both on .NET 10 against a throwaway "internal" service of our own, listening on loopback port 5401, with a fake key in its response. The safe endpoint used
SafeFetch.Create()
and returned 400 on
HttpRequestException
The list in
SafeFetch

covers the minimum ranges in OWASP's deny-list table and adds a few, such as the carrier-grade NAT range. It's the fallback for features that must accept any public URL. When you know the destinations, an allow-list is stronger.

rows.text: Other spellings, DNS records that point inside, redirects
Allow-list of known hosts, with fixed scheme, port and path
Rebinding, unless the resolved IP is checked too
You know every destination, such as a partner API
Resolved-IP check at connect time, redirects off
Internal services exposed on public addresses
The feature must accept any public URL, such as webhooks
Nothing the network can see, but they need upkeep

blocks.title: Close the metadata door at the platform

content.text: A check in code protects one feature; a platform setting protects every app on the machine. On AWS, require IMDSv2 so instances "only accept IMDSv2 calls", and block the metadata address in egress rules for services that never need it.

blocks.title: Don't send back what you fetched

content.text: Our wrong endpoint returned the internal JSON because it relayed the raw response. Our recommendation: return only what the feature needs, such as a re-encoded image after checking its type and size, and use generic errors, so a fetch that slips through leaks as little as possible.

blocks.title: Ask for less than a URL

content.text: OWASP's advice is "Do not accept complete URLs from the user". If users pick from known sources, take a source ID and a path, then build the URL yourself from an allow-list. OWASP is direct about the alternative: "Deny-lists are bypass-prone. Prefer allow-lists."
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Find every server-side fetch users can influence

content.text: Imports by URL, webhooks, link previews, PDF and HTML renderers, and XML parsers with external entities. Each one is a place where a user can choose a destination.

items.title: Allow-list wherever the destinations are known

content.text: Store the permitted hosts in configuration, fix the scheme, port and path in code, and reject anything else instead of trying to clean it.

items.title: Check the connection, not the string, for open URLs

content.text: Use a handler like
SafeFetch
: resolve, check every address, connect only to checked addresses, and keep redirects off.
Give fetching services their own outbound rules, deny internal ranges and the metadata address, and require IMDSv2 on AWS instances.
Cap size and time, validate the content type, and return a processed result rather than the raw response.
Key takeaways

items.text: SSRF turns your server into a proxy with your network's access; "inside our network" is the risk.
The OWASP Top 10:2025 maps SSRF to A01 Broken Access Control.
Checks on URL text miss other spellings, DNS records and redirects; check resolved IPs at connect time.
Prefer allow-lists and build URLs yourself; keep deny-lists as the fallback for open URLs.
Add network egress rules and IMDSv2, so one missed check doesn't expose cloud credentials.
